explanations: luna: The section contrasts two named springs by what their water does; 2:60 describes Moses striking a rock so twelve springs gush out and each group knows where to drink, a concrete communal spring scene. | terra: Twelve springs burst from the struck stone, every group knows its drinking place, and the people are told to eat and drink from God’s provision.
terra: Water bursts as rivers from some stones and emerges when others split, giving a concrete divine precedent for water released from an apparently closed source.
terra: The river test uses يَطْعَمْهُ for tasting or drinking its water, directly witnessing the source section’s dictionary claim that the ط ع م field extends to water.
terra: A drink of boiling water and painful punishment are placed in one sentence, bringing the source section’s hot drink and عَذَاب together without the sweet-water sense.

luna: The section contrasts punished thirst with a garden spring; 7:50 has the Fire's people beg the Garden's people to pour water on them, but they are refused. | terra: The people of the Fire ask the people of the Garden to pour down water or other provision, and are told that both are forbidden to them; the two communities and their radically different access to water meet in one exchange.

luna: The section treats the flowing spring as provision; 7:160 repeats the spring-gushing scene and explicitly tells the people to eat and drink from God's provision. | terra: Twelve springs gush from the rock and each tribe knows its drinking place, coupling a moving source with apportioned, ready access to water.

terra: Giving drink to pilgrims is treated as an organized human service and then weighed against faith and striving, extending the source section’s س ق ي act from divine afterlife provision to worldly hospitality.

luna: The section sets hot water as punishment against a flowing garden spring; 10:4 says the disbelievers receive a drink of boiling water and painful punishment, a direct parallel to that punitive drink. | terra: The disbelievers receive a drink of boiling water and painful punishment, another exact joining of infernal drink with the section’s punishment root.

terra: Joseph places the drinking vessel, السِّقَايَة, in his brother’s baggage; the drinking object and deliberate placement converge as in the source image, but here the placement initiates a test rather than garden service.

luna: The section stresses that springs share a name while their qualities differ; 13:4 says gardens are watered by one water yet differ in their produce, a specific parallel between common source and unlike outcomes. | terra: Different adjoining gardens and fruits are watered with one water yet differ in taste and quality, an inverse structural parallel to two springs sharing a name while their qualities diverge.
terra: Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure, so moving water appears as apportioned flow rather than a static supply.

luna: The section contrasts a garden's drink with punitive water; 14:16 says the condemned are given water of صَدِيد, a foul drink instead of a nourishing spring. | terra: The one facing Hell is given putrid water to drink, preserving the passive giving-to-drink while replacing the garden spring with a punitive source.

luna: The section describes water that cannot satisfy; 14:17 continues the painful drink of 14:16, saying the person struggles to swallow it and death comes from every side. | terra: The condemned person gulps the putrid water but can scarcely swallow it; this makes ease of drinking a sharp boundary from sweet, palatable water.
terra: God sends water from the sky, gives it to people to drink, and says they are not its keepers; the drink is ready, but its source is not theirs to command.

luna: The section places its flowing spring among garden furnishings; 15:45 says the God-fearing are in gardens and springs, the same reward setting. | terra: The God-fearing are amid gardens and springs in safety, a concise recurrence of the garden-spring scene.
terra: Water sent from the sky supplies human drink and vegetation for grazing, joining drinking water to the wider food provision generated by one source.
terra: Pure milk is brought from a hidden place between waste and blood and is palatable to drinkers, sharpening the section’s questions of source, purity, and ease of drinking.

terra: The opponents demand that the Prophet make a spring gush from the earth, closely paralleling the garden servants’ ability to make their spring gush while changing that gift into a challenge for proof.
terra: The demand continues with a garden of palms and grapes through which rivers must be made to gush abundantly, combining garden, flowing water, and human command of its course.

luna: The section's hot spring is a drink of punishment; 18:29 says the wrongdoers receive water like molten metal that scalds their faces, turning water into torment. | terra: When the people of the Fire seek relief, they are relieved with water like molten metal that scorches faces; expected refreshment becomes the evil drink itself.

luna: The section places moving water in a garden; 18:33 describes two gardens through which a river runs, a concrete garden-and-flowing-water parallel. | terra: A river is made to flow between two productive gardens, a worldly version of garden abundance organized around moving water.
luna: The section asks who could bring water if it sinks; 18:41 applies that danger to a garden's water, saying it may become sunken beyond recovery.
terra: Dhu al-Qarnayn reaches the sun’s setting place and finds it setting at a murky spring; it preserves عَيْن as a spring while moving it outside drinking and afterlife reward.
terra: Mary is consoled with a stream placed beneath her, a ready water source whose food-and-drink use is stated at 19:26.
terra: Mary is told to eat and drink beside the divinely supplied stream, another concrete joining of nourishment and water in one prepared setting.
luna: The section says the condemned remain hungry; 20:118 describes the garden where Adam will neither go hungry nor unclothed, a direct boundary against deprivation.
luna: The section makes thirst meet boiling water; 20:119 says Adam will not thirst or suffer the sun's heat in the garden, reversing thirst and scorching.

luna: The section's hot spring is punishment served as water; 22:19 says boiling water is poured over the heads of the disbelievers, making the drink an imposed torment. | terra: Boiling water is poured over the heads of the people of the Fire; the same hot liquid becomes external punishment rather than a drink.

luna: The section makes the hot drink bodily punishment; 22:20 completes 22:19 by saying it melts what is in their bellies and their skins. | terra: The poured boiling water melts what is inside their bellies and their skins, specifying the bodily effect of the hot source in 22:19.

luna: The section contrasts an available flowing spring with water that may disappear; 23:18 says water is settled in the earth and that God can take it away. | terra: Water descends in due measure, is lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; it states both the hidden storage and divine control presupposed by the ready spring.
luna: The section joins water to food as provision; 23:19 continues the account of water settled in the earth in 23:18 by describing gardens, abundant fruit, and eating from it.
terra: Livestock supply both what people are given to drink and what they eat, concretely joining drinking and feeding within one provided source.
terra: Mary and her son are sheltered on high ground with stable lodging and مَعِين, using the section’s visible flowing-water word for a worldly refuge.
terra: A thirsty person takes a mirage for water but finds none on arrival; it directly illuminates the section’s closing reversal in which anticipated good water fails the expectant face.
terra: God sends purifying water from the sky; the next ayah states that it revives land and is given to creatures to drink.
terra: Purifying rain is used to revive land and give many animals and humans drink, identifying fresh drinking water as purposeful provision.

luna: The section explicitly names عَذْبٌ as its dictionary form for sweet water, set against عَذَاب punishment; 25:53 calls one sea عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and the other bitter, making the water-quality distinction concrete. | terra: The source section’s dictionary sense عَذْب appears as one sea’s fresh sweetness, explicitly bounded from the salty, bitter sea despite their meeting.

luna: The section asks what happens when water is withdrawn; 26:57 describes Pharaoh's people being made to leave gardens and springs, a scene of lost abundance. | terra: Pharaoh’s people are expelled from gardens and springs, showing the same attractive scene as a worldly possession that can be removed rather than a settled reward.
terra: Abraham names the Lord as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, pairing the two acts that the section reads as one table and locating their source in God.

luna: The section presents springs as provision in a garden; 26:134 describes the worldly abundance of ʿĀd as gardens and springs, linking the spring image to provision. | terra: Hud reminds his people that their Lord aided them with gardens and springs, presenting the shared scene as a provision that calls for recognition.

luna: The section joins a spring with food and garden life; 26:147 describes gardens, springs, crops, and date palms in the provision promised to Thamud. | terra: Salih’s warning names gardens and springs among the abundance in which his people expect security, placing the scene at the boundary between gift and accountability.
terra: A rhetorical question names God as the sender of water that grows delightful gardens people could not grow themselves, matching the section’s question about who supplies flowing water.
terra: A rhetorical question asks who sends water from the sky and revives the earth, and the addressees answer “God”; it repeats the section’s demand to acknowledge the giver behind available water.
terra: Water is driven to barren land and brings forth crops eaten by livestock and people, tracing hidden water movement into food.

terra: Guests must not wait for the meal’s إِنَاهُ, its readiness, and must disperse once they have eaten, طَعِمْتُمْ; one table carries both the endpoint sense behind hot ءَانِيَة and the section’s food root.

terra: God makes a spring or fountain of molten copper flow for Solomon; the same spring-and-flow form carries a non-water substance, marking a concrete boundary around the section’s drinking springs and recalling molten punitive drink.

luna: The section's dictionary form عَذْبٌ means pleasant water, while 88:24 uses the cognate for punishment; 35:12 contrasts عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ water with salty, bitter water. | terra: One sea is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and easy to drink while the other is salty and bitter; the ayah states the water-quality boundary behind the section’s sweet-versus-punitive wordplay.

luna: The section's garden has a flowing spring; 36:34 says God made gardens and caused springs to gush in them, a direct garden-and-spring scene. | terra: Gardens of palms and grapes have springs made to gush within them, reproducing the garden-and-spring scene in the world as a sign.
luna: The section treats drinking and food as one provision; 36:35 completes the garden-and-spring scene of 36:34 by saying people may eat from its fruit.
terra: The garden inhabitants receive fruit and honor before the cup from a flowing source is passed to them at 37:45, so the drink belongs to a supplied table.

luna: The section connects drinking to a spring; 37:45 has a cup from مَعِين passed among the righteous, joining the cup to its source. | terra: A cup from مَعِين is passed around the garden; this same surah later gives the people of Hell a mixture of boiling water.

luna: The section contrasts the hot spring with garden drink; 37:46 describes the drink in the cup of 37:45 as white and delightful to drinkers. | terra: The cup from the preceding flowing source is white and delightful to drinkers, specifying the attractive quality withheld from the hot spring.

luna: The section contrasts punishment drink with garden provision; 37:47 completes the description of the cup in 37:45 by saying it causes no harm or loss of sense. | terra: The garden drink has no corrupting harm and does not exhaust or intoxicate, marking a concrete boundary from harmful infernal drink.

luna: The section sets garden drink against punitive food and water; 37:62 asks whether the garden's welcome or the tree of Zaqqum is the better provision, introducing the contrast that 37:66–67 completes. | terra: The ayah directly asks whether the garden’s hospitality or the tree of Zaqqum is better, setting the two tables against each other before the infernal food and boiling mixture are described.

luna: The section pairs food with hot water and says it cannot relieve hunger; 37:66 says the deniers eat from Zaqqum until their bellies are full. | terra: The people of Hell eat from Zaqqum and fill their bellies; the next ayah adds the boiling mixture that turns it into the section’s infernal meal.

luna: The section contrasts the garden spring with a punitive drink; 37:67 says a mixture of boiling water follows the Zaqqum meal. | terra: After eating from Zaqqum they receive a mixture of boiling water on top of it, making infernal food and hot drink one meal as in the source section.

luna: The section's garden spring is part of provision; 38:51 shows the garden's people reclining and calling for abundant fruit and drink. | terra: The garden inhabitants call for abundant fruit and drink, whereas the source section emphasizes cups already placed within reach before a request; the two scenes mark different modes of readiness.
luna: The section says the garden spring is renewed while hot water is fixed punishment; 38:54 says the garden provision does not run out.

luna: The section contrasts flowing spring water with a punitive drink; 38:57 makes the wrongdoers taste boiling water and ghassaq. | terra: The people of Hell are commanded to taste boiling water and foul cold fluid, another paired punitive beverage scene.

luna: The section contrasts moving spring water with water that may sink away; 39:21 describes rain made into springs in the earth, then plants drying and crumbling, showing the source's renewal and loss. | terra: God sends water down and conducts it through the earth as springs, a direct account of the hidden source and renewed movement behind visible flowing water.

luna: The section contrasts flowing water with a boiling source; 40:72 says the condemned are in boiling water and then fueled in the Fire. | terra: The condemned are dragged through boiling water and then burned, showing the hot water as an environment of punishment rather than a cup.
terra: God sends water from the sky in due measure and revives dead land with it, adding measured provision and renewal to the section’s moving-water side.

luna: The section connects cups with the garden; 43:71 shows golden dishes and أكواب being served there, with what the souls desire and eyes delight in. | terra: Golden dishes and أَكْوَاب are passed around the garden inhabitants, staging the source section’s cups as already supplied and served.
terra: Abundant garden fruit is eaten after the golden dishes and cups of 43:71, so the circulating vessels belong to a full table.

luna: The section asks who could restore a spring if it sank; 44:25 says Pharaoh's people left gardens and springs behind, marking the loss of water and provision. | terra: The drowned people leave behind gardens and springs; the shared scene becomes evidence of forfeited provision rather than enduring garden hospitality.
terra: The tree of Zaqqum supplies the object whose next ayah calls it the sinner’s food, beginning another infernal meal scene.

luna: The section describes an imposed, harmful food and drink; 44:44 identifies Zaqqum as the food of the sinner. | terra: Zaqqum is “the food of the sinner,” a direct counterpart to the exclusive dariʿ food before its boiling quality is described.

luna: The section makes eating part of punishment; 44:45 says the food boils in the bellies like molten dregs. | terra: The sinner’s food is likened to molten substance boiling in bellies, supplying the internal heat between its identification as food and its comparison with boiling water.

luna: The section's عين آنية is a spring whose heat has reached its limit; 44:46 compares the boiling in the belly to the boiling of حَمِيم. | terra: The sinner’s food boils like boiling water, letting the hot-water image enter the food itself before 44:48 pours boiling punishment over him.

luna: The section joins boiling water to عَذَاب punishment; 44:48 commands that boiling water from عَذَابِ الْحَمِيم be poured over the sinner's head. | terra: The command pours “the punishment of boiling water” over the sinner’s head, fusing عَذَاب and scalding water in one expression.

luna: The section sets the punished boiling spring against garden water; 44:52 says the God-fearing are in gardens and springs after the passage on Zaqqum and boiling water. | terra: The God-fearing dwell in gardens and springs, setting the same objects inside the secure reward announced in the preceding ayah.

luna: The section contrasts hot water with a renewed garden spring; 47:15 describes rivers of water that does not change, then the condemned being given boiling water. | terra: Within one ayah, the garden’s rivers of unspoiled water and other drinks are set against people made to drink boiling water; it condenses the section’s two-source polarity.

luna: The section associates a spring with the garden of the God-fearing; 51:15 repeats that they are in gardens and springs. | terra: The God-fearing are in gardens and springs, another direct recurrence of the reward scene defined by place and water source.

luna: The section sets hunger and boiling water against garden provision; 52:19 tells the people of the Garden to eat and drink in satisfaction. | terra: The garden command joins eating and pleasant drinking as recompense for deeds, a positive table opposite the hot drink and dariʿ table.
terra: Fruit and desired meat are supplied immediately before the companions pass a cup at 52:23, contributing the food half of that garden table.

luna: The section describes cups set ready in the garden; 52:23 has the garden's people pass a cup among themselves, a moving form of the same cup scene. | terra: Garden companions pass a cup among themselves with neither idle speech nor sin in it, linking the prepared cup to the larger surah 88 garden scene without futile speech.

luna: The section places cups among garden furnishings; 52:24 continues the cup scene with youths circulating among the garden's people in service. | terra: Youths kept for the garden people circulate among them, extending the shared cup scene of 52:23 into ready service.
terra: The earth is burst into springs until its water meets the descending flood at a decreed event; gushing water here overwhelms, bounding the controlled and welcoming garden spring.
terra: God “raised” the heaven and “set down” the balance in one ayah, directly staging the lexical opposition رَفَعَ and وَضَعَ that the section hears between raised couches and placed cups.
terra: God set the earth down for creatures, using the source section’s وَضَعَ root for deliberate availability on a larger scale than cups placed within reach.
terra: This ayah identifies the denied place as the Hell rejected by the criminals; 55:44 then describes their movement between it and endpoint-hot water.

luna: The section sets the hot spring against a flowing one; 55:44 places the deniers between the Fire and حَمِيمٍ آنٍ, making the spring itself part of punishment. | terra: The criminals move between Hell and حَمِيمٍ ءَانٍ, the exact endpoint-hot counterpart to the source section’s flowing garden spring.

luna: The section identifies the flowing spring with those who fear their Lord; 55:46 names those who fear their Lord's station and promises them two gardens, supplying the garden context for 55:50. | terra: Two gardens belong to the one who fears standing before the Lord; this identifies the stance of those whose two flowing springs appear at 55:50, opposite the criminals at 55:44.

luna: The section's ج ر ي note means water flowing; this ayah gives the God-fearing عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ, the paired, moving counterpart to 55:44's boiling water. | terra: The two gardens contain two springs that flow, فِيهِمَا عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ; both noun and motion directly amplify the section’s renewing spring.
terra: Each of the two gardens contains two kinds of every fruit after their two flowing springs are named, extending the paired-water image into paired provision.

luna: The section distinguishes a running spring from a spring at the heat's limit; a second garden pair in 55 has عَيْنَانِ نَضَّاخَتَانِ, another explicit pair of active springs. | terra: The second pair of gardens also has two springs, now described as gushing; this preserves the paired-spring scene while varying the kind of motion.
luna: The section links garden springs with nourishment; 55:67 continues the pair of gushing springs in 55:66 by naming the date palms and pomegranates of those gardens.
terra: Fruit, palms, and pomegranates follow the two gushing springs, supplying the food side of the second garden-and-spring scene.
terra: Immortal youths circulate around the garden people, identifying the service that bears the cups and ewers named in the next ayah.

luna: The section joins cups to the garden spring; 56:18 puts أكواب and أباريق beside a cup from مَعِين, joining serving vessels to visible flowing water. | terra: Cups, ewers, and a cup from مَعِين join vessel to visible flowing source; later hot drinking in this surah supplies the opposing water.
terra: The drink from the preceding flowing source causes neither headache nor loss of reason, a bodily reversal of the harmful waters on the section’s punitive side.
terra: Chosen fruit follows the cup from the flowing source, contributing food to the garden table whose drink appears at 56:18.
terra: Desired bird meat completes the food side of the service begun with cups and a cup from مَعِين.
luna: The section contrasts the hot spring with moving, replenishing water; 56:31 describes the people of the right receiving water poured out for them.
luna: The section presents food and drink as garden provision; 56:32 adds abundant fruit to the garden scene around the poured water.
luna: The section says the running spring renews; 56:33 says the garden fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden, a parallel of provision that remains available.

luna: The section says placed cups are the opposite of raised furnishings; 56:34 describes raised couches in the garden scene whose preceding verses mention poured water and enduring fruit. | terra: Raised furnishings reappear within a garden inventory, preserving the “raised” side of the placement opposition that structures the cups beside raised couches in surah 88.
luna: The section makes the hot spring a punishment drink; 56:42 places the condemned in scorching wind and boiling water, repeating the punitive heat-and-water pairing.
luna: The section opposes the hot spring to refreshing garden water; 56:44 says the punishment's shade is neither cool nor beneficial, clarifying that no relief comes from the scene.

luna: The section pairs punitive drink with food; 56:52 identifies the food of the deniers as fruit from the tree of Zaqqum, which the next verses make them eat and drink alongside. | terra: The erring deniers eat from the tree of Zaqqum; 56:54 then supplies their boiling drink, so this ayah contributes the meal’s food.

luna: The section says the punished food does not satisfy hunger; 56:53 says the deniers fill their bellies from Zaqqum, setting up the drink that follows. | terra: The deniers fill their bellies with Zaqqum before drinking boiling water, emphasizing the food portion of the paired punishment.

luna: The section's hot spring is an imposed drink; 56:54 says the deniers drink boiling water over the Zaqqum, directly joining the two sides of the punishment meal. | terra: They drink boiling water on top of Zaqqum, directly completing the same food-and-hot-drink table that the section sees in 88:5–6.

luna: The section contrasts running water with a drink that cannot quench; 56:55 likens the deniers' drinking to thirsty camels. | terra: They drink the boiling water like desperately thirsty camels, developing the manner of drinking after 56:54 identifies the liquid.
terra: The passage calls this food and drink their hospitality on the Day of Judgment, confirming that the preceding punishments form an offered table.

luna: The section treats drinking water as provision whose source is not human; 56:68 asks people to consider the water they drink, beginning the question of who supplies it. | terra: The hearers are made to look at the very water they drink, turning the garden cup’s contents into a question about ordinary dependence.

luna: The section asks who brings the spring water; 56:69 asks whether people or God sent down their drinking water from the clouds, naming its source. | terra: The next question asks whether people sent that water down or God did, matching the source question attached to مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ in the section.

luna: The section's root note ع ذ ب distinguishes sweet water from punishment; 56:70 says God could make drinking water أُجَاجًا, a bitter reversal of sweet water. | terra: God could make the water people drink bitterly salty, so a welcome cup depends on the same giver who can alter its quality.
terra: أَلَمْ يَأْنِ asks whether the due moment has arrived, preserving the reached-time or endpoint sense behind the source section’s description of ءَانِيَة as heat brought to its limit.

luna: The section asks who could restore water if it sinks away; 67:30 asks who will bring مَاءٍ مَّعِينٍ if their water becomes غَوْرًا, making dependence on a visible source explicit. | terra: The commanded question asks who could bring مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ if human water sank away, making the section’s ready flowing spring an explicitly divine provision.

luna: The section says cups are already at hand; 69:23 says the Garden's fruit clusters hang near, a parallel of provision made accessible. | terra: The high garden’s fruit clusters are brought near before its people are told to eat and drink, a close parallel to cups placed within reach before they are requested.

luna: The section pairs hunger with a drink that cannot satisfy; 69:24 tells the righteous to eat and drink in satisfaction, reversing that punishment. | terra: The people of the right are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they sent ahead, reversing the restrictive and painful meal in the source section.

luna: The section pairs food that fails to relieve hunger with hot water; 69:36 says the condemned have no food except غِسْلِين, a close parallel to the exclusive, non-nourishing food in 88:6–7. | terra: لَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ repeats the source section’s “no food except” construction while changing the sole infernal food from dariʿ to foul discharge.

luna: The section describes a food allotted to the condemned; 69:37 completes 69:36 by specifying that only the sinners eat it. | terra: Only sinners eat the foul food named at 69:36, specifying the eaters of that restrictive infernal fare.
terra: Abundant water would be given to drink if the people remained straight on the way, making plentiful water a conditional divine provision.

luna: The section makes the punishment meal a combination of drink and food; 73:13 names choking food and painful punishment, another scene where eating itself is part of torment. | terra: Choking food and painful punishment are named together, a compact parallel to the source section’s inedible infernal fare and greater punishment.

luna: The section describes drinks given to the people of the Garden; 76:5 says the righteous drink a cup blended with camphor, another specific garden beverage. | terra: The righteous drink a camphor-mixed cup, whose underlying spring is disclosed in 76:6; cup and source form one continuous garden image.

luna: The section's garden spring is available to drink from; 76:6 describes a spring from which God's servants drink and make it gush forth as they will. | terra: God’s servants drink from a spring and make it gush wherever they wish, joining drinking, spring, motion, and water placed at the garden people’s disposal.

luna: The section's ط ع م note treats eating as nourishment and includes water; 76:8 uses the food root for feeding the needy, orphan, and captive, a concrete act that relieves hunger rather than imposing it.
terra: Garden and silk are the recompense for patience, supplying the reward frame in which the silver vessels and cups of 76:15 are served.

luna: The section says the cups are placed within reach; 76:14 continues the garden scene by saying its fruit clusters are made easy to reach. | terra: Garden shade is brought near and fruit clusters are lowered within easy reach immediately before the vessels and cups are circulated, extending the section’s image of provision already positioned for use.

luna: The section says its root note for آنيَة gives a plural meaning vessels, unlike 88:5's hot-water adjective; 76:15 places آنية and أكواب together as the righteous are served. | terra: Silver ءَانِيَة vessels and أَكْوَاب cups are circulated together; this is the source section’s exact vessel homograph beside its exact cup noun.

luna: The section links cups to ready garden provision; 76:16 continues 76:15 by specifying the crystal-like silver vessels and measured cups, completing that serving scene. | terra: The glass vessels are silver and precisely measured, adding fitted measure to the cups circulated in 76:15.

luna: The section notes that the garden people are given a drink; 76:17 uses يُسْقَوْنَ for a cup blended with ginger, a specific counterpart to the punished drink. | terra: They are given drink from a ginger-mixed cup, repeating the source section’s passive giving-to-drink while changing the source from torment to reward.

luna: The section contrasts a flowing garden spring with the hot spring; 76:18 names Salsabil as a spring in that same garden drink scene. | terra: This ayah identifies the source of the preceding cup as a garden spring called Salsabil, completing the cup-to-spring relation.
terra: Everlasting youths circulate among the garden people, supplying the attendants implicit in the circulation of vessels at 76:15.

luna: The section contrasts the hot spring with provision in the garden; 76:21 says their Lord gives them a purifying drink, making the giver and the drink's quality explicit. | terra: Their Lord Himself gives them a purifying drink, making the ultimate giver explicit and reversing the punitive giving-to-drink in 88:5.

luna: The section contrasts sweet water with a hot spring; 77:27 says God gave people مَاءً فُرَاتًا, making pleasant drinking water the reverse of the punishment drink. | terra: God says “We gave you sweet water to drink,” making the provided drink fresh and palatable rather than the endpoint-hot drink of punishment.

luna: The section places a flowing spring in the garden of the God-fearing; 77:41 gives the God-fearing shade and springs after the passage on Hell's punishment. | terra: The God-fearing are among shades and springs, pairing shelter with the available water source on the garden side.
terra: Desired fruits stand between the garden springs of 77:41 and the command to eat and drink at 77:43, explicitly connecting source, food, and consumption.

luna: The section contrasts unrelieved hunger and hot water with garden provision; 77:43 tells the righteous to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did. | terra: The righteous are told to eat and drink pleasantly because of their deeds, making the garden table a reward rather than a punishment.

luna: The section opposes the hot spring to refreshing garden water; 78:24 says the people of Hell taste neither coolness nor drink. | terra: Hell offers neither coolness nor drink; the exception in 78:25 then reveals boiling water as the only “drink,” reversing normal refreshment.

luna: The section names a spring at the limit of heat; 78:25 specifies that the Hell dwellers receive only boiling water and ghassaq. | terra: The only drink allowed in Hell is boiling water and foul fluid; its restrictive exception reverses the freely available garden cup at 78:34.
terra: Gardens and grapes contribute the food setting whose brimming cup appears at 78:34, helping form the positive table opposed to the boiling drink earlier in the surah.

luna: The section's cups are placed ready in the garden; 78:34 describes a garden cup as كَأْسًا دِهَاقًا, an overflowing cup rather than a punitive drink. | terra: The garden has a brimming cup; in the same surah, the people of Hell have no drink except boiling water and foul fluid.

luna: The section notes يُسْقَوْنَ for a sealed pure drink; 83:25 gives the righteous that drink, reversing the punished people’s hot spring. | terra: The righteous are given sealed pure drink, repeating the source section’s passive drinking formula with a protected garden beverage rather than endpoint-hot water.

luna: The section cites the sealed drink in 83:25; 83:26 continues its description by saying its seal is musk, adding a concrete detail to that garden beverage. | terra: The sealed drink’s seal is musk and becomes an object of competition; this develops the “sealed” property named in 83:25 rather than leaving it an empty epithet.
